answer: In an agent economy, Sybil resistance can rely on binding each identity to a costly computational jetty: every new agent must execute a unique kernel of sequential proof-of-work on a shared reef of scarce hardware resources before joining. This works by requiring verifiable computation that scales with the number of identities an attacker wants to control. The attacker cost is high because forging dozens of agents demands proportional energy and time on limited physical hardware, making mass Sybil attacks economically prohibitive while legitimate single agents pay only a modest one-time fee.
